_2024_1_SCR_623.case_name: Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. v. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr.

matched_statutes.note: Discussed in context of 'forgery' requiring a fabricated document with intent to cheat.
Examined for fraudulent use of documents as genuine.

_2024_1_SCR_623.abstract_facts: The case involves allegations against the appellants of forgery related to obtaining a passport for a minor child. The appellants claim the actions were in line with instructions, but it is alleged that the signatures on the passport application were forged. The case arose amidst personal disputes between the appellants and the respondent husband, leading to competing legal actions.

propositions.text: For the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The fundamental elements of 'deceit' and 'damage or injury' are requisite for constituting the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: To establish the offence of forgery, the accused must have fabricated an instrument with the intention that it would be used for the purpose of cheating.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: 'Further investigation' under Section 173(8) CrPC requires obtaining new evidence and not merely reassessing existing material.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Under Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, an individual must knowingly furnish false information or suppress material information to be found guilty.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This precedent is adverse to the prosecution because the Supreme Court found no prima facie case for forgery under Sections 468 and 471 IPC on the facts before it, and it emphasized that forgery requires fabrication of an instrument with intent to cheat. In an anticipatory bail matter, the accused will cite this to argue that mere allegations of forged signatures or documentary irregularity, without stronger prima facie material, should not justify arrest.
use_for: Opponent may rely on the requirement in p3 that forgery needs fabrication of an instrument intended to be used for cheating, contending the present allegations do not yet show that threshold.
Accused may invoke the no-prima-facie finding on Sections 468 and 471 to argue that anticipatory bail should not be denied on a weak documentary dispute alone.
against: The prosecution can argue this case is factually distinguishable because the present case additionally involves IPC Sections 304A, 426, 427 and 506, and the Stage 4 assessment records a strong prima facie case under Section 471.

The Supreme Court's reasoning was tied to its own record and does not eliminate the possibility of custodial interrogation where forged documents, damage, intimidation, or death by negligence are alleged together.
distinguish: The precedent arose from a passport-related family dispute, whereas the present case includes allegations of mischief, criminal intimidation, and negligent death, not merely forgery allegations.
The input case's prima facie evaluation marks Section 471 as strong, so the prosecution can contend that the evidentiary posture here is materially different from the precedent's outcome.

defense.analysis: Quashing precedent establishing that dishonest intention at inception is mandatory for Section 420, directly supporting lack of prima facie criminality for bail.
use_for: Argue absence of dishonest or fraudulent intention at inception, which is an indispensable ingredient for Section 420 IPC
Establish that essential ingredients of forgery under Sections 468/471 are not satisfied prima facie (flagged as quashing precedent applicable to bail prima facie threshold)
against: The State may argue that the present case includes IPC 304A, 426, 427 and a stronger prima facie Section 471 allegation, so Mariam Fasihuddin cannot by itself neutralize the overall criminality assessment.
distinguish: This was not an anticipatory bail ruling; it was a merits determination on forgery/cheating in a passport-related factual matrix, so it cannot directly control the Section 438/BNSS 482 bail discretion.

The present case involves additional allegations of negligence, mischief, and intimidation beyond Sections 468 and 471, so the defence should use this authority only on mens rea and forgery ingredients.

_2018_7_SCC_581.case_name: Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj & Anr.
_2018_7_SCC_581.disposition: Appeals dismissed; acquittal of accused under Sections 465, 468, 471 IPC confirmed.

matched_statutes.note: Definition and basic ingredients of forgery
Forgery for the purpose of cheating
Using forged document as genuine

_2018_7_SCC_581.abstract_facts: The appellant filed a private complaint alleging that the respondent, an advocate, created a forged Power of Attorney (GPA) in the name of the appellant's deceased father and attempted to transfer property. The Supreme Court examined the legal requirements for establishing the offence of forgery under Sections 463, 464, and 468 IPC, specifically holding that a charge of forgery cannot stand unless the accused is established to be the maker or author of the false document.

propositions.text: Making of a false document under Section 464 IPC is the sine qua non for the offence of forgery under Section 463 and Section 468 IPC. Unless the prosecution establishes that the accused himself made or created the false document, a charge of forgery cannot be sustained.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Suspicion, however grave, cannot take the place of proof in criminal law; in allegations of forged property documents, the essential statutory ingredients under Sections 464 and 465 must be strictly established.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This authority is adverse to the prosecution because it reiterates that forgery under Sections 465/468/471 requires proof that the accused made or caused the false document to be made, and that suspicion cannot replace proof. In an anticipatory bail context, the prosecution can only use it defensively as a caution that it must show more than allegations of forged documents and must articulate concrete material linking the applicant to their creation or use.
use_for: Emphasize that the allegations are not a mere civil dispute if there is material showing the accused used or caused use of forged documents; the case underscores the legal importance of proving the forgery chain rather than relying on bare suspicion.
Argue that the prosecution must focus investigation on who authored, signed, or procured the forged document and how it was used, because Sections 468 and 471 turn on specific statutory ingredients.
against: The defense can rely on this case to argue that unless the applicant is shown to be the maker of the false document, the forgery charges are weak and anticipatory bail should not be denied on conjecture alone.
distinguish: The precedent arose in a quashing/merits setting, not an anticipatory bail proceeding, so its strict proof requirement cannot by itself answer the custody-focused bail question.

If the prosecution has material indicating use of forged documents or participation in their preparation, the case is distinguishable because it does not immunize a person who actively used or facilitated the forged document.

defense.analysis: Sheila Sebastian helps the defense on the core forgery principle that Sections 463/465/468 require proof that the accused made or caused the false document to be made, and mere suspicion is insufficient. However, it is a quashing/acquittal decision rather than an anticipatory bail precedent, so its value here is mainly to undermine prima facie forgery allegations, especially if the prosecution has not yet shown the accused as the maker of any false document.
use_for: Argue that the prosecution must first establish the Section 464 foundational ingredient—that the accused made or caused the false document—to sustain Sections 465/468/471 allegations.
Submit that absent clear material showing authorship/creation of the alleged false document, the forgery allegations remain only suspicious and cannot justify custody at the anticipatory bail stage.
against: The prosecution may rely on the fact that the precedent is not about bail and therefore does not control the discretionary Section 438/BNSS 482 inquiry.
distinguish: This case concerned final liability/quashing in a property-document forgery context, whereas the present matter is only at anticipatory bail stage; the defense can use it only as a prima facie ingredient-based authority, not as direct bail precedent.

_2022_10_SCC_51.case_name: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation & Anr.
_2022_10_SCC_51.disposition: Appeals disposed of with nationwide directions on bail and arrest guidelines.

matched_statutes.note: Anticipatory bail applications to be disposed of within six weeks
Strict compliance with Section 41A mandated

_2022_10_SCC_51.abstract_facts: The Supreme Court formulated comprehensive, binding guidelines categorizing criminal offences into four distinct categories (A, B, C, D) for the grant of regular and anticipatory bail. The judgment emphasized that arrest is a draconian power, personal liberty under Article 21 is paramount, and anticipatory bail applications must be decided expeditiously within six weeks.

propositions.text: For Category A offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years, bail should ordinarily be granted without taking the accused into custody if the accused cooperated during investigation and appeared on summons.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: For Category B offences carrying punishment of imprisonment for life (such as Section 467 IPC), applications for bail are to be dealt with on merits on appearance, balancing the gravity of the offence with personal liberty.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Arrest is a draconian measure which should not be used casually; courts must remember that personal liberty under Article 21 is a constitutional rule and incarceration is the exception.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

defense.analysis: Satender Kumar Antil strongly supports the defense on the anticipatory bail issue because it reaffirms that arrest is exceptional, Article 21 personal liberty must be protected, and cooperative accused persons should ordinarily not be taken into custody. However, it is only a background authority here because this case concerns general bail/arrest principles rather than the specific forgery/negligence allegations in the present matter.
use_for: Argue that anticipatory bail should be granted to protect personal liberty, since arrest is a draconian measure and incarceration is the exception.
Argue that if the accused has cooperated or is willing to cooperate with investigation, custody should not be treated as the default response.
against: The prosecution may rely on the fact that the judgment also recognizes category-based scrutiny, so seriousness of allegations such as strong prima facie forgery or mischief findings can still be pressed against bail.
distinguish: This precedent is not a property/title-specific or forgery-specific ruling; it lays down general bail/arrest principles applicable across offences, so it does not decide the merits of the alleged IPC Sections 465, 468, 471, 426, 427, 304A or 506 in this case.

_2025_9_SCR_982.case_name: Anna Waman Bhalerao v. State of Maharashtra
_2025_9_SCR_982.abstract_facts: The case concerns anticipatory bail applications filed by appellants, former government officials, following allegations of facilitating fraudulent property mutations based on forged documents during their tenure. The events occurred between 1996-1998, but the FIR was not filed until 2019. Attempts for anticipatory bail were made at both session and High Court levels, with interim protection granted intermittently. The Supreme Court was approached after the High Court's final rejection of anticipatory bail, amid concerns of inordinate delays in the case.

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail applications should be disposed of expeditiously, preferably within two months, except when delays are caused by the parties.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: In matters concerning personal liberty, bail courts must be sensitive and ensure constitutional ethos is upheld; prolonged delays in bail decisions are a denial of justice.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Custodial interrogation may be essential even in cases based largely on documentary evidence, to trace transactions and ascertain complicity.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The rejection of anticipatory bail by a High Court can be affirmed on appeal if interim protections were already extensively enjoyed without investigation cooperation.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This anticipatory-bail precedent supports the prosecution because the Supreme Court affirmed rejection where allegations involved forged documents and fraudulent use in a documentary/property context, and it expressly recognized that custodial interrogation may still be necessary to trace transactions and ascertain complicity. The defence may rely on the delay-related liberty observations, but the stronger prosecution point is that documentary evidence does not eliminate the need for arrest-stage interrogation in forgery-based offences under Sections 465, 468 and 471 IPC.
use_for: Argue that allegations of forged documents and their use as genuine make the case serious enough to justify denial of anticipatory bail, especially where Sections 465, 468 and 471 IPC are invoked.
Argue that even in a largely document-based case, custodial interrogation can be necessary to trace the document chain, transaction trail, and the extent of the accused's complicity.
against: The accused may invoke the Court's observations that anticipatory bail matters should be decided expeditiously and that prolonged delays in bail litigation are disfavoured.
distinguish: The precedent involved allegations around fraudulent property mutations by former government officials, while the present case also includes additional allegations of negligence, mischief, and intimidation, so the prosecution can rely on the forged-document ratio without being confined to the exact property-mutation setting.

_2020_2_SCR_1.case_name: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

matched_statutes.note: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 should not be limited by time, but courts may impose conditions.
Normal conditions in 438(2) can be imposed along with additional conditions based on the case.

_2020_2_SCR_1.abstract_facts: The Supreme Court was tasked with deciding on the conditions under which anticipatory bail, as provided under Section 438 of the CrPC, can be granted. In light of conflicting past judgments, the case was referenced to a larger bench to address whether anticipatory bail should be limited to a fixed period and whether it should terminate at the summoning stage or end of trial. The court emphasized the significance of liberty, noting unnecessary arrests and potential for harassment.

propositions.text: The protection granted under Section 438 CrPC should not ordinarily be limited to a fixed period. Conditions under Section 437(3) read with 438(2) should be imposed, but courts may add conditions based on crime severity.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The life of an anticipatory bail does not end when the accused is summoned or charges are framed, but can continue till end of trial unless circumstances necessitate otherwise.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail once granted can extend till the end of trial unless limited by conditions or circumstances warranting otherwise.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: An anticipatory bail order should not be blanket, granting protection from arrest for unspecified offences. It should be confined to the incident for which arrest is apprehended.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

defense.analysis: This is strong authority on the scope and liberal exercise of anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, supporting the defense’s Article 21/liberty-based plea and request for protection with appropriate conditions. However, it does not address whether the FIR allegations disclose forgery, negligence, intimidation, or any civil-versus-criminal character of the dispute, so it is principally a general bail framework case rather than fact-specific support.
use_for: Argue that anticipatory bail can subsist till the end of trial and need not be rejected merely because investigation is pending, subject to conditions.
Support the defense position that arrest should not be routine where liberty can be protected by cooperation and tailored conditions.
against: The Court cautioned that anticipatory bail should not be blanket and must be confined to the specific incident for which arrest is apprehended.
distinguish: The precedent is not about forgery, use of forged documents, negligence causing death, or mischief, so it cannot by itself negate the prima facie allegations in this case.
The case gives general Section 438 principles but does not establish that the present accusations are civil in nature or that mens rea is absent.

_2023_10_SCR_411.case_name: Pratibha Manchanda & Anr. v. State of Haryana & Anr.

matched_statutes.note: Anticipatory bail aims to safeguard individual rights while balancing public interest and ensuring a fair investigation.

_2023_10_SCR_411.abstract_facts: The appellants, alleging ownership of a land parcel in Gurugram, claimed never to have sold it or executed any power of attorney. They discovered that mutations were sought based on a purportedly forged sale deed and power of attorney from 1996. An FIR was lodged against the accused, who sought anticipatory bail from the High Court. The High Court granted bail, but the Supreme Court set aside the bail considering the need for custodial interrogation.

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail is designed to safeguard individual rights and prevent harassment from arrest, while balancing against public interest and ensuring the gravity of the offence is considered.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The custody of suspects is justified to ensure fair and thorough investigation when there are allegations of forgery and misappropriation of property.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The original GPA's absence raises doubts about the legitimacy of transactions claimed by the accused and underscores the need for investigation.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: In cases of alleged land fraud, thorough investigation by authorities is necessary, and anticipatory bail complicates uncovering the truth.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Bail cancellation should occur only with substantial reasons, but correcting an erroneous bail order differs.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: Directly supports prosecution: land fraud involving forged deeds warrants denial of anticipatory bail, and civil remedy is no bar.
use_for: Oppose anticipatory bail in fraudulent land conveyance involving forged documents and impersonation
Argue that pendency of civil proceedings or availability of civil remedy is no bar to criminal prosecution for land fraud
against: The defence may argue that the precedent arises from a land title/transaction dispute and therefore is factually different from the present case, which also includes negligence, mischief, and intimidation allegations.
distinguish: The precedent involved a land parcel and purportedly forged sale deed/GPA, whereas the present case includes additional IPC sections under 304A, 426, 427, and 506, so the prosecution can rely on it chiefly for the custodial-interrogation principle rather than exact factual identity.

_2009_8_SCC_751.case_name: Mohammed Ibrahim & Ors. v. State of Bihar & Anr.
_2009_8_SCC_751.disposition: Appeals allowed. Order taking cognizance under Sections 420, 467, 471 IPC quashed.

matched_statutes.note: Forgery for cheating
Using forged document as genuine

_2009_8_SCC_751.abstract_facts: The first appellant executed two registered sale deeds in favor of second and third appellants in respect of a parcel of land. The complainant alleged that the land belonged to him and that the first appellant, having no title, executed fraudulent sale deeds asserting ownership. A complaint was filed for offences under Sections 420, 467, 471, and 504 IPC. The Supreme Court examined whether executing a sale deed conveying property not belonging to the executant constitutes making a false document under Section 464 IPC, cheating under Section 420 IPC, or forgery under Sections 467/471 IPC.

propositions.text: When a person executes a document conveying property asserting that he is the owner thereof, knowing that he is not, he does not make a false document under Section 464 IPC, as he does not impersonate another or sign in another's name. Selling property one does not own does not constitute forgery.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Unless a false document is made as defined under Section 464 IPC, offences of forgery under Section 463 and aggravated forgery under Sections 467 and 471 IPC cannot be sustained.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Where a dispute is fundamentally a civil dispute over title to immovable property, the complainant cannot invoke the criminal process under Section 420 IPC to exert pressure on the accused.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: Adverse defense authority holding sale without title is not forgery under Section 464; prosecution must distinguish by proving actual document fabrication.
use_for: Distinguish the case by arguing that the present matter is not a mere land-title dispute but involves alleged forged documents and use of forged documents, which were not established in Mohammed Ibrahim.

Rely on the limited negative implication that the Supreme Court rejected criminalization only where there was no 'false document'; here, the prosecution can contend that Sections 465/468/471 survive if forgery is independently made out on the present facts.
against: The precedent is adverse to the prosecution to the extent it says selling or conveying property without title, by itself, does not amount to forgery or cheating.
distinguish: Distinguishable if the accused fabricated false ownership documents or impersonated the true owner, which falls squarely within Section 464

defense.analysis: Primary defense authority: executing a deed conveying land without title does not constitute a false document under Section 464, negating Sections 467/468/471.
use_for: Decisive landmark holding: Executing a sale deed conveying property not owned does NOT constitute 'making a false document' under Section 464 IPC
In the absence of a 'false document' under Section 464, charges under Sections 467, 468, and 471 IPC cannot stand
Civil dispute over ownership/title to agricultural land cannot be converted into criminal offences of cheating and forgery
against: The prosecution can argue that this case was decided in a quashing context, so it does not by itself determine bail entitlement where allegations under Sections 304A, 426, 427, and 506 are also invoked.
distinguish: Unlike Mohammed Ibrahim, the present matter also includes allegations under Sections 304A, 426, 427, and 506 IPC, so the defence can only use this precedent to attack the forgery/title-dispute component, not the entire FIR.

matched_statutes.note: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 should not be limited by time, but courts may impose conditions.
Normal conditions in 438(2) can be imposed along with additional conditions based on the case.

defense_precedents.abstract_facts: The Supreme Court was tasked with deciding on the conditions under which anticipatory bail, as provided under Section 438 of the CrPC, can be granted. In light of conflicting past judgments, the case was referenced to a larger bench to address whether anticipatory bail should be limited to a fixed period and whether it should terminate at the summoning stage or end of trial. The court emphasized the significance of liberty, noting unnecessary arrests and potential for harassment.

propositions.text: The protection granted under Section 438 CrPC should not ordinarily be limited to a fixed period. Conditions under Section 437(3) read with 438(2) should be imposed, but courts may add conditions based on crime severity.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The life of an anticipatory bail does not end when the accused is summoned or charges are framed, but can continue till end of trial unless circumstances necessitate otherwise.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail once granted can extend till the end of trial unless limited by conditions or circumstances warranting otherwise.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: An anticipatory bail order should not be blanket, granting protection from arrest for unspecified offences. It should be confined to the incident for which arrest is apprehended.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court
